rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds and reveal the occupied phi window plus any late hold elution. This should give a first map of retention and whether the key limitations are truncation, excessive compression, or near-unretained early peaks.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only score loss is from the last peak at 12.64 min; the goal is to shorten the run while preserving full credit on resolution. A narrower, higher-strength window with a shorter gradient should pull the late peak earlier but still keep the observed elution band inside the gradient.

We are very close to the ideal score, so the next move is a modest push to bring the last peak under 10 min while using a small temperature increase to offset the loss in resolution from the shorter gradient. This keeps the same successful phi window and tests whether the critical 6/7 pair still stays above 1.5.

The sharp loss at 45 C shows the critical 6/7 pair is temperature-sensitive, so move temperature in the opposite direction while keeping the faster 10 min gradient that already brings t_last below 10 min. This directly tests whether cooler conditions restore selectivity enough to keep all pairs above 1.5 and improve on injection 2.

Temperature clearly changes selectivity strongly, but tG = 10 min was too steep; increasing back to 12 min should recover slope-driven resolution while keeping the beneficial retention reduction from 45 C. This is the most direct test for getting the critical pair fully resolved and the last peak under 10 min at the same time.

Since temperature changes hurt the critical selectivity, stay at 40 C and instead raise phi0 to compress the early well-resolved region while preserving the late end of the window. This should shorten t_last modestly from the successful injection 2 without making the gradient steeper at the critical late cluster than necessary.

Injection 6 improved the score by raising phi0 while keeping all pairs fully resolved, so push that trend one more step to shave a bit more time off the last peak. The critical cluster still has margin, and this is a low-risk way to try to get t_last under 10 min without changing the successful temperature or overall gradient length.

You already have a perfect CRF, so this is a controlled robustness check that slightly trims the high-organic end while keeping the successful phi0, tG, and temperature fixed. It tests whether the last compound is still inside the gradient window and whether selectivity around the critical 6/7 pair remains intact with a narrower window.

A higher phi0 improved the score from injections 2 to 6 to 7, while lowering phi1 made the last peak later, so keep phi1 at 0.70 and test one more increase in phi0. This probes whether the method can stay fully resolved and perhaps remain at the maximum score with an even shorter effective run, while watching that the first peak does not become too close to unretained.

Injection 7 is already optimal, but after seeing that raising phi0 too far hurts the early pair and lowering phi1 delays the last peak, the clean orthogonal robustness check is to keep the successful phi0 and slightly raise phi1. This tests whether the last peak can be pulled earlier while preserving both the early 1/2 pair and the critical 6/7 separation.

Injection 7 already reaches the maximum score, so use remaining runs to probe an alternative robust region: a slightly shallower gradient to protect the critical 6/7 pair, combined with higher temperature to offset retention and try to keep t_last under 10 min. This tests whether a second 1.000-capable condition exists with more margin on the critical pair.

The failure at 45 C confirms temperature strongly affects the critical 6/7 pair, so test the opposite direction with a shallower gradient that should increase slope-based separation while the lower temperature may restore selectivity. This explores whether a cooler, slightly longer gradient can still keep t_last under 10 min while improving margin on the critical pair relative to injection 7.

Temperature excursions and longer gradients have been detrimental, so stay at 40 C and test a wider, slightly stronger window around the perfect condition. Lowering phi0 from 0.20 should restore margin for the early pair while raising phi1 from 0.70 may pull the last peak earlier, probing whether another fully resolved 1.000-capable setting exists nearby.

You now have a second perfect method, and the critical 6/7 pair remains just above threshold, so slightly increasing phi1 tests whether the last peak can be moved earlier without losing full-resolution credit. This explores the upper edge of the successful window while keeping a safer phi0 than injection 7 for the early peaks.

With 0.15/0.75/12/40 already at CRF 1.000 and the critical 6/7 pair near the threshold, a slightly longer gradient should add selectivity margin while likely still keeping the last peak under 10 min because phi1 is relatively high. This tests whether there is a more robust perfect method than injection 13.

The 14 min gradient showed extra slope margin but too much time penalty, so the natural remaining bracket around the perfect 12 min condition is 10 min at the same phi window and temperature. This directly tests whether the high-phi1, lower-phi0 window can keep the critical 6/7 pair above 1.5 while giving a shorter fully resolved run.

At 0.15/0.75/10/40 the run is fast but the critical 6/7 pair is under-resolved; lowering phi1 should reduce gradient steepness and may recover that pair while likely keeping t_last below 10 min. This tests whether the 10 min gradient can be made fully resolving by narrowing the window at the high-organic end.

The remaining unexplored bracket around the best method is shortening tG to 10 min while keeping the successful phi window and temperature from injection 7. This tests whether the exact best-window condition can still achieve full resolution at a shorter run, or confirms that 12 min is the minimum slope needed for the critical 6/7 pair.

The data show 10 min is too steep and 12 min is optimal around 40 C, but the combined effect of a slightly higher phi1 with a longer gradient has not been tested. This run checks whether the extra slope margin from 14 min can offset the stronger high-organic end enough to maintain full resolution while still keeping the last peak under 10 min.

Both perfect methods are at 40 C, but temperature effects were only tested at other windows; this run checks whether the broader low-end window that worked at 0.15/0.75/12 can tolerate a modest increase in temperature when paired with the gentler 0.15/0.70 window. It is a final orthogonal probe for an alternative fully resolved method with different thermal conditions.

Since higher temperature consistently collapses the critical 6/7 pair, test the opposite at the already perfect 0.15/0.75/12 window to see whether cooler conditions provide a more robust selectivity margin while still keeping the last peak near or below 10 min. This is the cleanest remaining thermal check around a known optimum.

With two perfect 12 min methods established and temperature variation clearly harmful, use a nearby isothermal-selectivity control by lengthening only tG at the best phi window. This checks whether injection 7 sits at the minimum gradient time for full resolution and gives a direct robustness comparison against the shorter optimum.

This fills the last obvious slope-control gap near the other perfect window, isolating the effect of longer tG without the confounding high-phi1 end. It should confirm whether 12 min is also the minimum time-optimal fully resolved setting for the 0.15/0.70-0.75 region.

The last untested corner near the successful 0.20/0.70 and 0.20/0.75 windows is the fast 10 min gradient with the higher phi1. This will confirm whether the stronger high-organic end plus steeper slope further degrades the critical 6/7 pair, completing the local map around the best method.

This is the last untested fast-window corner around the second perfect method, combining the safer low phi0 with the stronger high-end window at the shortest gradient time.
